kurz: Why the question of how much is enough shapes the end result more than any choice of fund.

bloecke.md:
Money performs two very different tasks. You can use it to buy things, and you can use it to give yourself choices. The benefit of things is immediately visible and quickly fades. Choices cannot be seen, but they become more valuable with every year. Both are paid for out of the same budget. Because only the things stand out in everyday life, they are almost always given priority.

Morgan Housel developed this idea in a book in 2020. It does not contain a single formula and yet explains more about the investment results people actually achieve than most textbooks. His first thesis is that no one is crazy. People make decisions about money based on their own life story rather than on spreadsheets. Someone who spent their first working years in a bear market will judge shares differently for the rest of their life from someone whose first ten years in the capital market brought only rising prices. In 2011, Malmendier and Nagel showed empirically that the capital market return a household has *personally experienced* predicts its later willingness to take risks better than the entire historical return. This insight helps you avoid dismissing other people's behaviour as stupidity and helps you examine your own.

A car in the driveway stands for money that has been spent and says nothing about money that is still there. Wealth is the difference between what someone earns and what they show. That is why you can see riches, but not wealth. Other people's visible lifestyle is therefore the worst yardstick imaginable.

## Enough as a target

The hardest financial skill is to stop moving a goal further and further upwards once it has been set. Choosing investments, timing and tax optimisation are easier by comparison. Housel describes Rajat Gupta and Bernie Madoff, who had fortunes in the hundreds of millions and risked everything, and asks what they did it for. The mistake rarely lies in greed in the moral sense; in most cases a fixed target is missing. Without deciding how much is enough, that point is inevitably never reached. The yardstick is then always the next higher group, and after each step up, a new group takes its place.

[[Enough]] can be calculated in concrete terms. Every permanently higher standard of living also has to be financed permanently. At a withdrawal rate of 3.5% a year, every additional euro spent each month ties up capital of around €343.

bloecke.titel: Capital needed for permanently higher consumption

bloecke.md: The table shows why pay rises so rarely make people rich. They have a double effect, but only if the extra money is not spent straight away. A higher savings rate increases the annual inflow and at the same time lowers the target wealth. This is because the target wealth is a multiple of *spending*, not of income. Because of this double effect, the savings rate has a stronger impact than the return in every realistic illustrative calculation.

bloecke.titel: Years to reach the target wealth by savings rate
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation starting from zero, with a 4% real return and a target wealth of 28.6 times annual spending (3.5% withdrawal), deliberately without the statutory pension, inheritances and taxes. The pension and inheritances would shorten the bars, taxes would lengthen them. The proportions between the bars would also change, but their order would stay the same.

bloecke.md:
## Status consumption and habituation

According to an observation by Housel, people who buy an expensive car in order to be admired overlook the fact that the admiration is directed at the car and not at the driver. These buyers therefore bear the costs, while the recognition goes to the object.

Behind this lies [[hedonic adaptation]]. The reference point rises with the level of consumption. A bigger car, a bigger flat or a better restaurant feels better for a few weeks to months. After that, it becomes the norm, from which you once again compare yourself with a higher level. The effect on wealth, by contrast, is permanent, because the higher level of consumption remains while the feeling of happiness fades. If a pay rise is spent entirely on lifestyle, well-being afterwards is back at its starting level, but the capital needed for your own independence has risen.

If an extra €400 net a month is spent entirely on recurring fixed costs, the capital needed for financial independence rises by around €137,000 (€4,800 / 0.035). Meanwhile, the amount saved each month does not increase. Fixed costs are more dangerous than one-off purchases. A more expensive car costs the extra amount once, whereas a more expensive tenancy, a lease or a subscription costs money every month and is hard to reverse.

## Saving without a goal

In Germany, saving is almost always promoted with a purpose, such as a car, a kitchen, your own home or retirement. Housel, by contrast, recommends saving part of your money expressly without a purpose. This recommendation has a rational basis and follows the logic of options. Money without a designated use is an option on future action. The value of an option rises with uncertainty, that is, in situations in which plans are no longer worth anything.

The practical benefit can be measured by the decisions you do not have to make under pressure. With freely available money, you can ride out a dismissal, turn down a poor job offer, bridge a period of caring for a family member or hold out for three months without any assignments. For investing, what matters is that investors with liquid reserves do not have to sell during a market decline. The MSCI World lost around 57% between 31 October 2007 and 9 March 2009. Investors who needed money during this phase and therefore had to sell turned a fluctuation into a permanent loss.

In German practice, this money therefore belongs in an instant-access savings account or in money market funds and not in the equity portion. Deposits are protected by law up to €100,000 per customer and institution under Section 8 EinSiG (Deposit Guarantee Act). Interest income is subject to the flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) of 25% plus the solidarity surcharge under Section 32d(1) EStG (Income Tax Act). For a typical emergency fund, the saver's allowance (Sparerpauschbetrag) of €1,000, or €2,000 for joint assessment, covers a considerable part of this income (Section 20(9) EStG).

## Expected value and individual path

An example from the debate about ergodicity shows the mathematical side of risk. In a bet, the *entire* wealth staked changes by +50% or −40% each round, each with a probability of 50%. The expected value per round is 0.5 × 1.5 + 0.5 × 0.6 = 1.05, that is, +5%. For an individual player, the path over time looks different. One gain and one loss together give 1.5 × 0.6 = 0.9, so per round √0.9 ≈ 0.9487, or around −5%. The average across many parallel paths rises, while the typical individual path falls.

bloecke.titel: Expected value and typical path, €100 over 20 rounds
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation based on the multiplicative coin toss of ergodicity economics, with +50% or −40% per round. Ensemble average 1.05^n, time average 0.9^(n/2). Wealth that is repeatedly staked in full typically follows the lower line.

bloecke.md: This leads to a risk rule that applies in every market environment. Ruin is ruled out first, and only then is the return optimised. For a private household, ruin rarely means a total loss on the stock exchange. It usually takes the form of a forced sale at the wrong time, a securities-backed loan during a market decline, cluster risk with your own employer (salary and shares from the same source) or property financing without a buffer for the end of the fixed-rate period and for repairs. Taleb calls the principle the barbell. The largest part is invested very safely, a small part deliberately speculatively, and the deceptive middle is avoided.

A portfolio holds €600,000 in an equity ETF, 50% of which is unrealised gain. Each year, €21,000 is withdrawn (3.5%).

- Taxable gain portion of the units sold: 21,000 × 50% = €10,500
- Partial exemption (Teilfreistellung) of 30% for equity funds held as private assets under Section 20 InvStG (Investment Tax Act): −€3,150 → €7,350
- Saver's allowance (Section 20(9) EStG): −€1,000 → €6,350
- Flat-rate withholding tax of 25% plus solidarity surcharge, together 26.375% (Section 32d(1) EStG): around €1,675

Around €19,325 is available net. The effective tax burden on the withdrawal is therefore about 8% rather than 26.375%. Only the gain portion is taxed, and only 70% of it because of the partial exemption, while the saver's allowance exempts a further €1,000. Advance lump sums (Vorabpauschalen) that were already taxed during the accumulation phase (Section 18 InvStG) further reduce the gain (Section 19 InvStG). Church tax and personal circumstances change the result.

bloecke.unter: The upper levels are more valuable and yet are bought less often than the lower half.

stufen.text: Deciding for yourself what you work on, where and for how long.
Being able to say no to assignments, relocations, bosses or poor prices.
No forced selling in a decline, no overdraft, no sleepless night over a bill.
Housing, food, insurance, running costs. The higher levels build on this.

bloecke.text: Controlling your time is the highest dividend money pays.
bloecke.quelle: Morgan Housel, The Psychology of Money (2020)

bloecke.md:
Three numbers and one rule are written down once and dated.

1. The emergency fund as an amount expressed in months of net spending, held liquid in a separate account.
2. Annual spending as last year's actual figure rather than a wished-for figure.
3. The target wealth, that is, annual spending divided by the chosen withdrawal rate.
4. A rule for pay rises under which a fixed share of the net increase (for example, half) goes automatically into your monthly savings before it becomes visible in your current account.

The numbers do not have to be exact. Their value lies in having a target that does not move along when income rises.

The research is less robust than popular summaries suggest.

- Easterlin (1974) found that within a country, wealthier people are on average more satisfied. When a country's average income rises over decades, however, average satisfaction hardly rises. Stevenson and Wolfers contradicted this in 2008 using other data. The debate is open.
- Kahneman/Deaton (2010) found in US data that *emotional* well-being levelled off above an annual income of around $75,000, while people's *evaluation* of their own lives continued to rise.
- Killingsworth (2021), using smartphone measurements, found no such kink. The joint follow-up study by Killingsworth, Kahneman and Mellers (2023) resolved the contradiction with the finding that well-being continues to rise with income for the majority, but levels off above a range of around $100,000 for an unhappy minority.
- Brickman and colleagues (1978) compared lottery winners and accident victims. Their study is the most cited on adaptation, but it is based on very small numbers of cases and accordingly has little explanatory power.

What the findings have in common is that the relationship is logarithmic rather than linear. Each further doubling of income brings roughly the same increase in satisfaction. A jump from €30,000 to €60,000 therefore has a similar effect to one from €120,000 to €240,000. All the amounts mentioned come from US surveys and cannot be transferred directly to German conditions.

Part of the investment decision cannot be captured in any table. For this, Housel distinguishes between reasonable and rational. A mathematically optimal strategy that your nerves cannot stand is worse than a slightly suboptimal one that you stick with. An investor with a 100% equity allocation who sells at −40% has acted wrongly in practice, despite a mathematically correct allocation. Your own pain threshold is thus an input to the portfolio decision and not a character flaw. It should be measured as honestly as costs and taxes.

mitnehmen: Money buys things and choices, and only the choices become more valuable over time.
Wealth is the difference between what is earned and what is displayed; it is therefore invisible, and comparing yourself with others tells you nothing.
At a 3.5% withdrawal rate, every euro spent permanently each month ties up around €343 of capital, which is why the savings rate has a double effect and a stronger one than the return.
Part of your savings should deliberately serve no goal, because liquidity is an option on future action whose value rises when plans become worthless.
Ruin is ruled out first and the return optimised afterwards, because the expected value does not describe the path an individual investor experiences.

begriffe.text: A target wealth or level of spending fixed in advance that does not move along when income or surroundings rise. Without this fixed reference point, the yardstick automatically shifts to the next higher comparison group.
The observation that a higher level of consumption becomes the new normal after a few weeks to months. The feeling of happiness returns to its starting level, while the costs remain permanently.
The automatic growth of spending in step with income. It lowers the savings rate and at the same time raises the target wealth required. It thus makes financial independence harder in two ways.

Property of a random process in which the average across many parallel paths equals the average of a single path over time. Multiplicative wealth paths are not ergodic. That is why a bet with a positive expected value can ruin an individual investor.
The benefit of available money that, regardless of the interest it earns, lies in the actions it makes possible and in the forced decisions it avoids. It rises with uncertainty.
